title: Basil's new city
hook: Basil of Caesarea built a place of care for the poor and sick, and his friend called it a new city

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius' community: monks sharing work, prayer and one table. Your line: together is harder, and better.

"I will pull down my barns, and build greater." That's the rich man in one of Jesus' parables, in Luke's Gospel. His harvest is huge, so he plans bigger storage, and that night his life is asked of him. Basil, then a priest in Caesarea, in what's now central Turkey, and later its bishop, preached on that line to his own people. In his time, a famine came to his city, and the rich, like the man in the parable, had full barns. Basil had a sermon, a pulpit, and a gift for making people uncomfortable. By the end he's built, on the edge of town, what his close friend would call a new city.

The famine first. His friend Gregory tells it, in a speech in Basil's memory. Basil opened the storehouses of those who had them, by the force of his preaching. He gathered the hungry in one place and served them himself, with his own hands, alongside his helpers. In his sermon on the barns, Basil pushes hard. In paraphrase: the bread you keep in store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the one without one. He isn't asking for leftovers. He's asking whose the extra really is. Then he builds. Outside Caesarea, Basil put up a whole complex: lodging for travelers and strangers, a place for the poor, care for the sick, with people to nurse them and workers to keep it going. A local governor was apparently uneasy. Basil wrote to him: what harm does this do the state? We're housing strangers and caring for the sick. Go a little way out of the city, Gregory says in paraphrase, and look at the new city, a storehouse of devotion, where the rich put their surplus. And he singles out the people others avoided: those with the disease that disfigured skin and drove sufferers out of town. Basil didn't keep his distance. He greeted them, embraced them, even kissed them, as brothers. Not a building, but a bishop bending down to kiss someone everyone else had sent away.
screen: `THE FAMINE: HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.`
`THE BREAD YOU KEEP IS THE HUNGRY'S.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place near you where people are cared for when sick or poor, a clinic, a hospice, a shelter, a food bank, and remember it if it ever carried you. Basil asked his governor what harm the place did; ask instead what it runs short of, blankets, cans, a driver, a thank-you for the night staff. If you pray, pray for the sick there and those who care for them.
Basil. The bishop of Caesarea who built a place of care outside his town, for strangers, the poor and the sick, that his friend Gregory called a new city.
Your line: a city of mercy. Built just outside the city. That's day seven hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian orders run hospitals, clinics, hospices, shelters and food banks, and church members give to and volunteer in them.

notes: The index hook says 'one of the first hospitals for the poor and sick'; per the claims rule the script and hook avoid 'first'. Confirm, or restore the index hook.
Famine relief: Gregory, Oration 43.35–36 (opened storehouses by preaching, gathered the hungry, served with his own hands). Paraphrased; confirm.

The line 'the bread you keep belongs to the hungry; the coat ... belongs to the one without one' is paraphrased from Basil's homily; confirm which homily it belongs to (Homily on Luke 12:18 or the homily 'To the Rich').
Letter 94 to the governor Elias defending the buildings: paraphrased; confirm the governor's unease and details.

Oration 43.63: 'go forth a little from the city and behold the new city, the storehouse of piety'; and Basil greeting and kissing those with leprosy. Paraphrased; confirm. The script avoids the word 'leper'.
The hook does not claim the barns sermon came before or during the famine; some date it to the famine. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'his best friend' (superlative) became 'his close friend'; varied the stock 'start with' teach opener; the practice now draws on Basil's own question instead of repeating day 764's 'money, time or hands' list.

Second editor pass: 'who gave the speech at Basil's funeral' became 'in a speech in Basil's memory'. Oration 43 is traditionally called the funeral oration but is usually thought to have been delivered some time after Basil's death, not at the funeral; the script no longer places it there.

Audit pass: FACT FIX. The hook called Basil a bishop at the time of the famine; Gregory (Oration 43.34–36) places the famine while Basil was still a presbyter (he became bishop in 370). Hook now says 'then a priest ... and later its bishop'. Practice no longer repeats day 765's give-away-from-your-closet practice; it now asks what the place of care runs short of.
